payload.message:
Good morning! Time for your daily style check.

1. **Read Inventory:** Load `closet.json` to see what I currently own.
2. **Read Deals:** Load `latest_clothing_deals.md` (if it exists) to get the deals that were found yesterday evening.
3. **Check Weather:** Use the `exec` tool to run: `curl -s "wttr.in/Bentonville+AR?format=%l:+%c+%t+%w"`
4. **Outfit Pick:** Recommend the best combination from my `closet.json` for today's weather. Explain why.
5. **Format Output:** Output a final summary containing the 🌤️ Weather, the 👔 OOTD, and the 🛍️ Deals (copied from the file). This output will be automatically sent to my Telegram.

Execute the 'viral-researcher' skill (Full Cycle).
1. Read `research/weekly_log.md` to see what trended this week.
2. Pick the best topic.
3. Generate the full 'Deep Dive' markdown file (like the H1B example).
4. Send the user a Telegram message with:
   - The Topic Headline
   - A summary
   - The content of the file (or a confirmation it was saved).

Research trending immigrant topics for 'Borderless'.
1. Scan Reddit (r/expats, r/immigration, r/AskAnAfrican) and Google News for "viral" debates. Focus on: Money, Family Pressure, Mental Health, Return Anxiety. (Avoid purely visa/legal news).
2. Save a brief summary of the top 3 topics to `research/log/weekly_log.md`.

Reminder: The "Communication Temptation" Protocol

This involves deliberately setting up the home environment to make vocalization necessary.

• Visible But Inaccessible: Use clear, plastic bins with tight lids for favorite snacks. Wait for the child to bring the bin to you, then model the word "Open" or "Cookie".
• Piece-by-Piece Delivery: Instead of giving a bowl of goldfish crackers, give one at a time. This creates 20–30 "learning trials" in a single snack session.
• Interrupted Chains: If the child is playing with a track, withhold one piece of the track. When they reach the gap, model the word "Track" or "Help".

Use the 'message' tool to send this exact text to Telegram user 8510312060 (channel="telegram"):

Reminder: Time-Delay and Mand-Model

This mechanism shifts the burden of communication onto the child while providing a safety net of prompts.

• Anticipatory Pausing: During a highly preferred activity like swinging or tickling, stop the activity abruptly. Wait 5 seconds while looking expectantly at the child. If they make any sound, immediately restart the activity.
• Graduated Prompting: If the child does not respond to the pause, provide a partial prompt (e.g., "S..." for "swing") before giving the full model.

Reminder: High-Probability (High-P) Request Sequences

To build "behavioral momentum" and encourage a child who is hesitant to speak:

• The Sequence: Ask the child to perform 3 simple actions they already enjoy and can do easily (e.g., "Give me five," "Touch your nose," "Clap").
• The Vocal Target: Immediately after the third successful motor action, deliver the vocal prompt for a new word. The momentum of compliance from the motor tasks often carries over to a vocal attempt.

Use the 'message' tool to send this exact text to Telegram user 8510312060 (channel="telegram"):

Reminder: Stimulus-Stimulus Pairing (SSP)

For children who are not yet imitating sounds:

• The Pairing: Sit with the child and make a silly, simple sound like "Pop!". Immediately after you make the sound, blow a bubble or give a tickle.
• The Goal: Do not ask the child to repeat the sound. Over dozens of repetitions, the sound "Pop" becomes associated with the fun of bubbles. Eventually, the child will say "Pop" spontaneously because the sound itself has become reinforcing to them.

Goal 1: Thelma will initiate a peer interaction (e.g., greeting, asking to play, joining ongoing play, or sharing an item) in a naturalistic setting using gestures or her AAC device. Instructions: Teaching Peer Interaction at Home 1. Set up a play opportunity. Have your child and their sibling play near each other with a preferred toy or activity (blocks, dolls, a game, etc.). 2. Create a reason to interact. Give the sibling a toy your child likes, or have them start playing with something interesting. 3. Prompt the interaction if needed. Encourage your child to interact by modeling or gently prompting a greeting, asking to play, or sharing. This can be done using gestures or their AAC device (for example: “hi, ” “play, ” “my turn, ” or “want to play?”). 4. Give time to respond. Pause for a few seconds to allow your child to attempt the interaction independently. 5. Reinforce the interaction. When your child initiates with their sibling, provide praise (e.g., and allow the play activity to continue. “Great asking to play!”) 6. Keep practice short and positive. Practice during natural play times for a few minutes at a time so interactions stay fun and successful. Tip: The goal is simply to encourage your child to start the interaction. Any attempt using gestures or their AAC device should be praised and supported.

Encourage your child to begin the task and remain engaged with the materials. 4. Provide encouragement as needed. If your child starts to lose focus, gently redirect them back to the activity by pointing to the task or reminding them to finish. 5. Reinforce completion. Goal 6: Thelma will independently complete a 3-step clean up routine after meal time (e.g., throw trash away, place dish in sink, wiping the table). Instructions: Teaching the After-Meal Clean-Up Routine 1. Explain the routine. After your child finishes eating, remind them of the clean-up steps: 1) Wipe the table → 2) Throw trash away → 3) Put plate in the sink. A visual reminder or saying the steps together can be helpful. 2. Prompt the first step if needed. Encourage your child to start by wiping the table. If they need help, you can point to the table or model the action. 3. Guide through the remaining steps. After the table is wiped, prompt your child to throw the trash away, then place the plate in the sink. 4. Allow independence when possible. Give your child a moment to complete each step on their own before providing help. 5. Provide praise for completing the routine. When your child completes the steps, provide praise such as “Great job cleaning up after your meal!” 6. Practice consistently. Practice this routine after meals so it becomes a predictable part of the daily routine. Tip: Keeping the steps in the same order each time helps your child learn the routine and become more independent over time.

Goal 7: Thelma will use her AAC device for a variety of communicative functions independently 10 times per hour. Instructions: Supporting AAC Communication at Home The goal is for your child to use her AAC device frequently to communicate throughout the day. The device helps her express her needs, wants, comments, and feelings in a way others can understand. Ways to Encourage AAC Use 1. Keep the device nearby and available. Make sure the AAC device is always within reach so your child can use it during daily activities like meals, playtime, and routines. 2. Create opportunities to communicate. Pause during activities to give your child a chance to request or comment using her device. For example, before giving a snack or starting a preferred activity, wait a few seconds to encourage communication. 3. Model using the device. You can show your child how to use the AAC by pressing buttons and saying the word out loud (for example, pressing “eat, ” “play, ” or “help”). This helps them learn how the device can be used. 4. Respond to communication attempts. When your child uses the device, respond right away and praise the attempt (for example, “Nice job telling me you want play!”). 5. Encourage communication across situations. AAC can be used for many purposes, such as: ○ Requesting items or activities ○ Asking for help ○ Commenting or sharing ○ Greeting others ○ Saying “all done” Why This Is Important Frequent use of the AAC device helps your child communicate their needs instead of using behaviors to express frustration or wants. The more opportunities your child has to use the device, the more comfortable and independent they will become with communication.
